title: One name, four types
description:
Write four overloads of `describe`, each returning a `std::string` that names the type and shows the value:

| Call | Returns |
|---|---|
| `describe(42)` | `"int: 42"` |
| `describe(2.5)` | `"double: 2.500000"` |
| `describe(true)` | `"bool: true"` |
| `describe(std::string_view{ "hi" })` | `"text: hi"` |

`std::to_string` turns a number into text (for a `double` it always shows six decimals).
hints: Each overload has the same name and a different parameter type. The compiler chooses by the type of the argument.
stretch: Try calling `describe("hi")` with a plain string literal. It picks the `bool` version! A literal is a pointer, and pointer-to-bool is a built-in conversion that beats the conversion to `std::string_view`. Add an overload taking `const char*` to fix it (pointers, written with `*`, are lesson 4.04).
